title: Serving, inference and production LLM systems
summary: Composite primary: rohitg00 Phase 17 (all 29 lessons mapped, concepts + quizzes) paired lesson-by-lesson with real-tool labs on vLLM, llama.cpp, LiteLLM, Locust, Langfuse, k3d and Toxiproxy. Cloud fundamentals moved to M21; distributed training/CUDA is an optional specialist track. GPU labs run on free Colab/Kaggle T4s or fall back to llama.cpp on CPU; no card needed anywhere.

practice.title: KV-cache budget, checked against vLLM (real-tool lab for rohitg00 17/04, 17/06)
practice.brief: Free GPU route: Google Colab or Kaggle notebooks (T4, no card; Kaggle needs phone verification; quotas change) with a <=3B model; CPU fallback: llama.cpp. Compute by hand the KV-cache bytes for an 8B Llama-style model (layers, KV heads, head_dim, fp16) at 4k context x 16 sequences; then for the 1-3B model you can run, predict max concurrent sequences and compare with vLLM's startup log ('# GPU blocks' / KV cache size). Toggle `--enable-prefix-caching` and measure TTFT on 20 requests sharing a 1,500-token system prompt.
practice.done_when: KV.md shows the formula 2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes x tokens with numbers; predicted vs logged KV capacity within 15%; TTFT p50 with and without prefix caching reported.

quiz.prompt: Decode is typically:
quiz.explain: Each token reads all weights and the KV cache for little compute; prefill is the compute-heavy phase.

quiz.prompt: Continuous batching improves on static batching by:
options: Adding/removing sequences every iteration so finished requests do not block
quiz.explain: Iteration-level scheduling keeps the GPU busy.

quiz.prompt: PagedAttention mainly reduces:
quiz.explain: Fixed-size blocks avoid reserving max-length contiguous memory.

quiz.prompt: Why does a long shared system prompt benefit from prefix caching, and what breaks the benefit?
rubric: KV for the shared prefix is computed once and reused, cutting prefill time/TTFT and compute.
Breaks if the prefix varies (timestamps/user data at the start), or cache is evicted under memory pressure.
Put static content first, dynamic content last.

quiz.prompt: Why can raising the batch size increase throughput but lower goodput?

practice.title: Find the knee (real-tool lab for rohitg00 17/22)
practice.brief: No-card path: Locust from your laptop against llama.cpp `llama-server` locally (CPU) or vLLM in Colab. Prompts sampled from a distribution (e.g. lognormal input lengths), streaming on. Run ramp and spike tests; run Locust with multiple worker processes and watch load-generator CPU.

quiz.prompt: A soak test mainly finds:
quiz.explain: Hours of steady load reveal memory leaks, fragmentation, log growth.

quiz.prompt: Identical prompts in a loop overestimate performance because:
options: Prefix caching and uniform lengths do not reflect real traffic
quiz.explain: Real traffic has varied lengths and fewer cache hits.

quiz.prompt: If your load-generator CPU is at 100%:
options: Your results may be measuring the client
quiz.explain: Scale out the generator before trusting numbers.

quiz.prompt: State your capacity plan as 'N replicas for X RPS at p95 < Y' and list its assumptions.
rubric: Gives concrete N, X, Y derived from measured per-replica knee with headroom.
Assumptions: prompt/output length distribution, cache hit rate, model/quant, hardware, traffic peak factor.

practice.title: Queue-aware autoscaling on k3d (real-tool lab for rohitg00 17/03)
practice.brief: No-card path: k3d on CPU with llama.cpp `llama-server` as the model pod. Add a startup probe sized to model load time, put a small FastAPI queue in front with max depth 20 that returns 503 when full, export queue depth to Prometheus, and scale with an HPA on that metric (prometheus-adapter or KEDA; a simulated metric is acceptable if adapters are too heavy - document it).
practice.done_when: Under a Locust spike, `kubectl get hpa -w` shows scaling on queue depth; a deliberately low startupProbe threshold reproduces the restart loop and the fixed value cures it; 503 rate during the spike reported alongside p95 for accepted requests.

quiz.prompt: A startup probe protects slow-loading models from:
options: Being killed by the liveness probe during warm-up
quiz.explain: Liveness/readiness are held off until startup succeeds.

quiz.prompt: GPU utilisation is a poor HPA signal for LLM servers because:
options: It measures kernel duty cycle, not how saturated the request queue is
quiz.explain: A GPU can read 100% busy while latency is fine, or vice versa.

quiz.prompt: Load shedding (fast 503) under overload:
options: Protects latency for accepted requests and avoids cascading failure
quiz.explain: Better to reject quickly than time out everything.

quiz.prompt: What does a cold start cost when scaling an LLM from 0 to 1 replica, and how do you hide it?
rubric: Node provision + image pull + weight download + load into memory/HBM + engine init/warm-up (minutes for big models).
Hide with min replicas/warm pool, pre-pulled images, cached weights on local disk/volumes, smaller/quantized models, queueing with honest 202/503.
States the cost trade-off of keeping warm capacity.

quiz.prompt: Disaggregated prefill/decode pays off least when:
options: Prompts and outputs are both short
quiz.explain: KV transfer overhead dominates when there is little prefill or decode work to separate.

quiz.prompt: Round-robin load balancing hurts cached inference because:
options: Requests sharing a prefix land on replicas without that KV cache
quiz.explain: Cache-aware/sticky routing preserves prefix hits.

quiz.prompt: Mobile/edge LLM inference is mostly bound by:
quiz.explain: Same reason as decode on GPUs: weights must stream through memory per token.

quiz.prompt: Your team runs one 8B model on two GPUs at 20 RPS. Which of today's five techniques would you adopt first, if any, and why?
rubric: Likely cache-aware routing/prefix caching first (cheap, immediate TTFT win) or none.
Explains disaggregation/LMCache/TRT-LLM need larger scale, long contexts or specific hardware.
Ties the decision to measured bottleneck.

practice.done_when: Tests pass: rank gradients equal; accumulation equivalence assert; resumed loss curve continues from the saved step (plot); README explains which collective DDP uses and its bytes per step.

quiz.prompt: DDP synchronises:
quiz.explain: Each rank has a full model copy; gradients are averaged with all-reduce.

quiz.prompt: FSDP/ZeRO-3 reduces per-GPU memory by:
options: Sharding parameters, gradients and optimizer states
quiz.explain: Each rank holds only its shard and gathers parameters when needed.

quiz.prompt: Gradient accumulation simulates:
quiz.explain: Sum gradients over micro-batches before stepping.

quiz.prompt: Why does all-reduce bandwidth limit scaling beyond one node?
rubric: Inter-node links (Ethernet/InfiniBand) are much slower than intra-node NVLink.
Gradient bytes per step are fixed by model size, so communication time can exceed compute.
Mitigations: overlap comm/compute, gradient compression, larger batches, hierarchical/sharded strategies.

practice.title: Profile, then fuse
practice.brief: Free GPU route: Google Colab or Kaggle notebooks (T4, no card; Kaggle needs phone verification; quotas change) with a <=3B model; CPU fallback: llama.cpp. Profile one step of a small transformer with torch.profiler (Colab T4), export a Chrome trace, name the top-3 ops. Implement Triton fused softmax from tutorial 02 and benchmark against torch.softmax for 3 sizes.
practice.done_when: Chrome trace committed; PROFILE.md names top ops with % time; benchmark table (GB/s) for Triton vs PyTorch with a sentence on why fusion helps a memory-bound op.

quiz.prompt: Kernel fusion helps memory-bound ops mainly by:
options: Reducing round-trips to GPU global memory
quiz.explain: Intermediate results stay in registers/shared memory.

quiz.prompt: In the PyTorch profiler, a large gap between CPU dispatch and GPU kernels suggests:
quiz.explain: Consider CUDA graphs, torch.compile or larger batches.

quiz.prompt: Triton lets you write GPU kernels at the level of:
options: Blocks/tiles of data with automatic scheduling inside a block
quiz.explain: It abstracts intra-block thread management.

quiz.prompt: You profile inference and 40% of time is in many tiny elementwise kernels. What do you try, in order?
rubric: torch.compile/operator fusion first (cheap).
CUDA graphs / larger batches to amortise launch overhead.
Custom fused Triton kernel only if still dominant; re-measure each step.

capstone.title: Serve, measure, break, recover
capstone.brief: Serve an open model (vLLM on a Colab/Kaggle T4, or llama.cpp on CPU) behind your gateway (quotas, cache, fallback, Langfuse traces). Run ramp, spike and soak tests; report TTFT/TPOT p50/p95/p99, goodput and cost per 1k requests; identify the bottleneck with evidence; apply one optimisation (quantization, prefix caching, batching knob or cache) with before/after and quality re-evaluated; demonstrate canary + rollback under load. No-card path: everything local + free notebook GPUs.

levels: Realistic prompt-length distribution; percentiles not means; client bottleneck ruled out; raw data committed
Named bottleneck (prefill, decode, queue, memory, client) supported by metrics/graphs
One change with controlled before/after and quality re-evaluated
Rollback under load with no SLO breach beyond the stated window; overload sheds gracefully
Cost/1k requests, break-even vs API, SLOs, runbook and DR note
